rv.q: Jake Gyllenhaal and Tom Sturridge deliver scorching performances that can stand alongside anything on the New York stage so far this season.
And the performances remain riveting.
Both actors deliver their monologues with devastating emotional precision, creating an evening that feels both intimate and universal in its exploration of love, loss and the fragility of life.
The writing in these separate monologues is excellent, as are the solo performances by Tom Sturridge and Jake Gyllenhaal.
This production doesn’t slow down long enough to provide the necessary undergirding for “A Life” to pack the emotional punch it’s aiming for.
Jake Gyllenhaal is a stage animal for sure. But he needs more feral turf in ‘Sea Wall/A Life.’
But with Gyllenhaal in the role, likable though he is, it seems perversely self-centered and generic: a memorial play that functions as an erasure.
But universal truths, unless conveyed in inspired artistic form, can become bland banalities.

The audience loved “A Life,” but I found it intolerable, and I spent the last half-hour longing to hurry home and watch a Humphrey Bogart movie to wash its sickly sweet taste out of my mouth.

If to only witness these immensely gifted actors transform themselves completely before your eyes, “Sea Wall / A Life” is a must-see.
It is an astoundingly convincing portrayal.

And yet, that culture of optimism is just the comfort Payne provides at the end of an emotional theatre-going experience, through Abe's connection with a popular song that most audience members will know, and perhaps even Alex can take comfort from.
They are among the most heart-wrenching words I’ve ever heard in a theater, and likely to linger in your mind for days and days.
That finale lifts an already exceptional production to an even higher plane.
Sturridge’s exquisitely raw, delicate performance has so thoroughly captured our imagination and empathy that the revelation surpasses a gut punch, becoming a full blow to the heart.
The words alone are enough to transport you to that ominous sea wall where tragedy inevitably strikes.
Sea Wall/A Life is a refreshing Broadway exercise; shorn of fuss, décor, and movement, we are invited to simply sit and listen to the telling of stories.
There may not in fact be any self-evidently memorable lines nor an undeniably unforgettable journey.
Experiencing the monologues in a larger venue does not detract from their dramatic power because they are directed squarely at the audience, treating it as a participant and a confidante.
The strength of these monologues lies precisely in their modesty.
This could happen to any one of us, they seem to be saying; but Gyllenhaal and Sturridge have made that perfectly clear in their performances.
It would be nice to see these linked monologues by Jake Gyllenhaal and Tom Sturridge in an intimate setting.
Even the starry solo turns of Jake Gyllenhaal and Tom Sturridge can’t relieve the monotony of seeing Stephens’ “Sea Wall” and Payne’s “A Life” back to back with an intermission.
It’s the creation of life and the taking away of that same gift that is simplistically engaging and direct, even when these men are at a loss for the right words.
The reason to see them remains the excellent work of the stars.
Art can shed light on our deepest sorrows and traumas, but these two brief plays are more like glib gestures in the direction of loss.

cn.t: Gyllenhaal and Sturridge deliver emotionally intense performances in this pairing of monologues about grief and fatherhood, though critics split on whether the modest, sobering one-acts justify a Broadway run beyond the actors' star power.

sg.ra: SeatPlan, TickPick and Headout all converge: center rows D-K sit at a perfect distance to take in the whole stage without craning. Row A is called out as too close for comfortable viewing. Dress Circle overhangs at Orchestra row L and the Mezz overhang only becomes obvious at row R without significantly cutting the stage, so the middle band is protected. 2017 ATG restoration upgraded legroom throughout.

SeatPlan flags Dress Circle A-B center as offering unobstructed sightlines and the 'front few rows of the Center Dress Circle' as premium; rows D-F center are repeatedly called out as great-value seats with full sweep of the stage. The 258-seat section has a good rake and generous legroom. Balcony overhang only becomes obvious at row J and doesn't cut into the stage, so every row is usable.

SeatPlan describes Balcony rows A-B center as hanging close enough for detailed views and reports sightlines 'better than average' for a third level. Rear rows G-H are the cheapest in the house. Rake is very good, but legroom is tighter than the rest of the theater and the top of the stage may be cut by the balcony's angle. AVFMS user at G110 noted that some in-audience action isn't visible from rear balcony.
